Integrated distribution models with mvgam

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/articles/idm.Rmd
idm.Rmd

Species are often monitored by several protocols at once. A structured count route, an occupancy survey and opportunistic sightings each observe the same underlying intensity of individuals, filtered through a different sampling process. Integrated distribution models fit one likelihood per protocol and tie every likelihood to that shared intensity (Fithian et al. 2015; Isaac et al. 2020; Miller et al. 2019). Each protocol then informs the environmental response that drives the intensity.

mvgam fits such a model as a multivariate formula. Each protocol gets its own bf() with the family and link that describe its sampling process. One trend_formula describes the log-intensity they share. This article simulates three protocols observing one species, then compares how well the joint model and each protocol alone recover the species’ response to an environmental gradient. The article on one latent process with several observation models covers the same machinery from the angle of the latent state.

The data

We simulate one species observed monthly for eight years. Its log-intensity combines a bell-shaped response ff to an environmental index with an autoregression at lags 1 and 12:

log⁡λt=α+f(envt)+zt,zt∼Normal(ϕ1zt−1+ϕ12zt−12,σ), \log \lambda_t = \alpha + f(\text{env}_t) + z_t, \qquad z_t \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\phi_1 z_{t-1} + \phi_{12} z_{t-12},\ \sigma),

with ϕ1=0.55\phi_1 = 0.55, ϕ12=0.30\phi_{12} = 0.30 and σ=0.35\sigma = 0.35. The response ff peaks at env =0.4= 0.4.

Each protocol links to λt\lambda_t through its own sampling process. Counts along a route surveyed with effort EtE_t are Poisson with mean λtEt\lambda_t E_t. The term offset(log_effort) carries the effort. An occupancy survey of a plot of area AA detects the species when at least one individual is present. With a Poisson number of individuals in the plot, the detection probability is pt=1−exp⁡(−λtA)p_t = 1 - \exp(-\lambda_t A). This is the inverse complementary log-log link, under which cloglog(pt)=log⁡λt+log⁡A\text{cloglog}(p_t) = \log \lambda_t + \log A (McCullagh and Nelder 1989). With bernoulli(link = "cloglog"), the occupancy record shares the log-intensity of the counts, offset by log⁡A\log A. Opportunistic sightings arrive at rate λt\lambda_t thinned by an unknown, constant observer effort. Treated as a thinned Poisson process, they take a free intercept that absorbs the log thinning and leaves the shape of ff identified (Fithian et al. 2015; Renner et al. 2015).

set.seed(2026)
n_t <- 96
env <- as.numeric(scale(cumsum(rnorm(n_t, 0, 0.3))))
f_env <- function(x) 1.5 * exp(-0.5 * (x - 0.4)^2) - 0.4

z <- numeric(n_t)
for (t in seq_len(n_t)) {
  z[t] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.35) +
    (if (t > 1) 0.55 * z[t - 1] else 0) +
    (if (t > 12) 0.30 * z[t - 12] else 0)
}
lambda <- exp(0.5 + f_env(env) + z)

effort <- runif(n_t, 0.5, 2)
area <- 0.25
log_thinning <- -0.8

idm_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n_t),
  series = factor("species1"),
  env = env,
  log_effort = log(effort),
  count = rpois(n_t, lambda * effort),
  pa = rbinom(n_t, 1, 1 - exp(-lambda * area)),
  po = rpois(n_t, lambda * exp(log_thinning))
)

The joint model

The three bf() calls share the trend formula, which holds a smooth of env and the autoregression at lags 1 and 12:

joint_formula <-
  bf(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), family = poisson()) +
  bf(pa ~ 1, family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog")) +
  bf(po ~ 1, family = poisson())
trend_formula <- ~ s(env, k = 8) + AR(p = c(1, 12))

mod_joint <- mvgam(
  joint_formula,
  trend_formula = trend_formula,
  data = idm_data,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  chains = 4, seed = 2026, silent = 2
)

plot(type = "series") draws each protocol’s record, its distribution and its autocorrelation:

plot(mod_joint, type = "series")

The three simulated records: counts, occupancy detections and opportunistic sightings.

summary() reports one intercept per protocol and the trend parameters they share:

summary(mod_joint)

The autoregressive coefficients and the innovation SD each cover the values used to simulate the data. Because only eight annual cycles inform it, the lag-12 coefficient (0.19 [-0.14, 0.49]) is the least certain of these.

The intercepts carry what the shared trend leaves to each protocol. Because the linear predictor of every protocol holds the same log⁡λt\log \lambda_t, the trend cancels from the difference between two intercepts. The difference between the occupancy and count intercepts estimates log⁡A\log A. The difference between the sightings and count intercepts estimates the log thinning:

b <- as_draws_df(
  mod_joint,
  variable = c("b_count_Intercept", "b_pa_Intercept", "b_po_Intercept")
)
contrasts <- data.frame(
  `log area` = b$b_pa_Intercept - b$b_count_Intercept,
  `log thinning` = b$b_po_Intercept - b$b_count_Intercept,
  check.names = FALSE
)
round(t(apply(contrasts, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))), 2)
#>               2.5%   50% 97.5%
#> log area     -1.75 -1.45 -1.17
#> log thinning -1.09 -0.90 -0.72

The simulated constants are log⁡0.25=−1.39\log 0.25 = -1.39 and −0.8-0.8. Both intervals cover them. Neither constant was given to the model.

pp_check() draws one panel per protocol. Rootograms compare the frequency of each count. Bars give the share of each outcome of the binary occupancy record:

pp_check(mod_joint, ndraws = 50)

Posterior predictive checks for each protocol.

The environmental response

plot(type = "smooths") draws the smooth of env on the log-intensity scale:

plot(mod_joint, type = "smooths")

The smooth of env from the joint model, with its 95% credible interval.

conditional_effects() carries that smooth through each protocol’s observation model, with the trend state held out and effort set to one:

ce <- conditional_effects(mod_joint)
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot(ce, plot = FALSE), nrow = 1)

Expected count, detection probability and sighting rate along env from the joint model, with 95% credible intervals.

To ask what the integration gains, we fit each protocol alone with the same trend formula:

fit_one <- function(formula) {
  mvgam(formula, trend_formula = trend_formula, data = idm_data,
        control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
        chains = 4, seed = 2026, silent = 2)
}
mod_count <- fit_one(
  bf(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), family = poisson())
)
mod_pa <- fit_one(bf(pa ~ 1, family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog")))
mod_po <- fit_one(bf(po ~ 1, family = poisson()))

Each model’s linear predictor over a grid of env values shares the shape of ff. Subtracting its value at the median of the grid removes the protocol’s intercept and the trend state. The joint model’s predictor is taken from the count response:

grid <- seq(min(env), max(env), length.out = 60)
ref <- which.min(abs(grid - median(grid)))
newdata <- idm_data[rep(1, length(grid)), ]
newdata$env <- grid
newdata$log_effort <- 0

response_draws <- function(fit, resp = NULL) {
  lp <- posterior_linpred(fit, newdata = newdata, resp = resp)
  lp - lp[, ref]
}
fits <- list(
  "Joint" = response_draws(mod_joint, resp = "count"),
  "Counts alone" = response_draws(mod_count),
  "Occupancy alone" = response_draws(mod_pa),
  "Sightings alone" = response_draws(mod_po)
)
truth <- data.frame(env = grid, f = f_env(grid) - f_env(grid[ref]))
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
  q <- apply(fits[[nm]], 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
  data.frame(model = nm, env = grid, lo = q[1, ], med = q[2, ],
             hi = q[3, ])
}))
curves$model <- factor(curves$model, levels = names(fits))
ggplot(curves, aes(env)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#DCBCBC") +
  geom_line(aes(y = med), colour = "#8F2727", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = f), data = truth, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "env", y = "Shift in log-intensity")

Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals of the response to env from the joint model and from each protocol alone. The black line is the simulated response.

Three summaries compare the four curves: the root mean squared error of the posterior median against the simulated response, the mean width of the 95% credible interval and the posterior median of the env value at which each curve peaks.

recovery <- t(vapply(fits, function(draws) {
  q <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
  peak <- grid[apply(draws, 1, which.max)]
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((q[2, ] - truth$f)^2)),
    `Interval width` = mean(q[3, ] - q[1, ]),
    `Peak env` = median(peak))
}, numeric(3)))
round(recovery, 2)
#>                 RMSE Interval width Peak env
#> Joint           0.17           0.67     0.38
#> Counts alone    0.17           0.75     0.32
#> Occupancy alone 0.62           1.23     2.02
#> Sightings alone 0.41           0.85     1.07

The joint model and the counts alone track the response with root mean squared errors of 0.17 and 0.17. Intervals are narrowest in the joint fit. Against the simulated optimum of 0.4, the sightings alone put the peak at env 1.07 and the occupancy record alone at env 2.02. One binary outcome per month constrains the intensity weakly.

Forecasts

forecast() extends the shared state past the last month and passes it through each protocol’s observation model. The new data hold unit effort and env at its final observed value. type = "expected" returns the expected count, the detection probability and the expected sightings:

future <- data.frame(
  time = n_t + 1:12,
  series = factor("species1"),
  env = env[n_t],
  log_effort = 0,
  count = NA, pa = NA, po = NA
)
fc <- forecast(mod_joint, newdata = future, type = "expected")
plot(fc)

Expected values for each protocol over the training months and a 12-month forecast. Points are the observations.

The three forecasts share one future for the state. Once the held-out records arrive, score() evaluates them protocol by protocol.

When protocols disagree

We fit the joint model on the premise that every protocol observes one intensity through one response to env. Two violations are common. The first is a mismatch of species. An opportunistic record that mixes the target with an easily confused congener observes a different intensity (Fithian et al. 2015 analyse this case). The second is a mismatch of habitat. If the occupancy plots sample habitat the count route never visits, the two protocols see different responses to env. A joint smooth then averages them.

The single-protocol fits diagnose both mismatches. A protocol whose response disagrees with the others, beyond what its interval allows, is a candidate for a response of its own. That response moves to the protocol’s observation formula, for example bf(pa ~ 1 + s(env, k = 5), family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog")), while the shared response stays in the trend formula. Koshkina et al. (2017) develop this combination of presence-background and occupancy data with imperfect detection.

Summary

An integrated distribution model in mvgam is one call. Each protocol’s family and link express its sampling process. The shared trend pools what every protocol says about the intensity. In this simulation, intervals on the environmental response were narrowest in the joint fit. Fitted alone, the occupancy record put the optimum at env 2.02, against the simulated 0.4.
